slides.hook: AI laws are rising fast. **Your governance cannot wait**

slides.title: Law is moving faster than your roadmap
slides.body: Legislative and regulatory activity on AI has surged since 2016. Boards now expect evidence that AI use is mapped to emerging rules, not future intent.

slides.title: Principles are converging, not optional
slides.body: Most policy frameworks repeat the same themes: privacy, accountability, safety, transparency, fairness and human oversight. Your internal standards should mirror this spine.

slides.title: Hard law vs soft law hits delivery
slides.body: Statutes, licences, standards and policies now mix. Teams need clear guidance on which rules are binding, which are advisory, and how they translate into builds, tests and approvals.

slides.title: Regulators care about the full lifecycle
slides.body: Governance must cover who owns risk, what is in scope, when controls apply in the lifecycle, and how they are implemented through models, tools and human checkpoints.

slides.title: Sector rules make reuse harder
slides.body: AI rules are arriving in finance, health, security, transport and public services. A model that is compliant in one context may be non-compliant in another without redesign.

slides.title: Global activity, local accountability
slides.body: International bodies are building common guidance, but enforcement is domestic. Multinationals need a single governance spine that can absorb divergent national rules.

slides.title: Control problems are now board issues
slides.body: Long-term safety, explainability and misuse are no longer academic topics. They shape risk appetite, model choices, data strategy and the approval to scale automation.

slides.line: If AI law stepped up a level tomorrow, would you be ready?

caption:
AI regulation is no longer a horizon issue.

Executives now need provable governance, not principles on a slide. The organisations that win will treat regulation as a design input, not a last-mile hurdle.
